R001.text: Fix arbitrary x∈ℝ^n and t>0. H002 is smoothness on the open set Ω. Repeatedly apply M009 over ℝ to the zero extension of u on Ω with both smoothness orders ∞; since ∞+1=∞ this gives smoothness of its iterated derivatives on Ω. Evaluation of these continuous multilinear derivatives on fixed coordinate vectors gives the ordinary smooth partial derivatives. M002, over ℝ at (x,t), with order 2, then gives equality of time-space mixed second derivatives, by evaluating the symmetric second derivative on the time and j-th spatial coordinate vectors. Finite sums, scalar products and products of smooth real components are smooth, so e and e_t are continuous. M001 applied along the time line to u with itself gives ∂_t(u·u)=2u·u_t. H004 says u·u=1 throughout Ω; its derivative is zero. Thus u·u_t=0. This calculation is valid at every point of Ω, so the identity holds throughout Ω, not only at the chosen point; it may therefore be differentiated along any time line in Ω.

Choose a from H005 at (x,t). By F001 and the finite-sum definition of the scalar product, u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=u_t·(a u)=a(u_t·u)=0. This uses no derivative or regularity of the selected scalar. For completeness, M001 along time, applied to u and u_t, differentiates the identity u·u_t=0 and yields |u_t|²+u·u_tt=0. Applying the same product rule first to u·u=1 and then to u·∂_{x_j}u=0 along any spatial coordinate line gives u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting the normality equation with u and using u·u=1 therefore gives a=Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². Since this calculation uses only the defining equation for a, it holds for every scalar satisfying it.

M001 applied along time to u_t with itself gives ∂_t|u_t|²=2u_t·u_tt. Applied to ∂_{x_j}u with itself, it gives ∂_t|∂_{x_j}u|²=2∂_{x_j}u·∂_t∂_{x_j}u; the mixed-derivative equality of F001 replaces the last factor by ∂_{x_j}u_t. Differentiating the finite spatial sum gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. Together with F001 and F002 this proves every clause of the output for the arbitrary point. The witness a does not escape: the assertion about it is universal conditional on its displayed equation.

R002.text: Fix t0>0 and define J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Its endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2, so H006 supplies a compact C with u=q outside C for all times in J. Apply M008 with real-valued function x↦|x| on C. The norm is continuous, so there is a real upper bound on these norms. Increasing it to a strictly positive number larger than it gives a real R>0 with |x_j|≤|x|<R for all x∈C and all j. Consequently a suitable R with C⊂(−R,R)^n exists, also when C is empty.

Choose R as in F001 and put Q=[−R,R]^n. In the coordinate order this is a closed order interval; M014 gives its compactness in finite real coordinate space. It is closed and therefore Lebesgue measurable. M013 with both endpoints constant −R,R gives |Q|=(2R)^n<∞. Here H001 provides positive finite dimensions. M011 for any real constant on Q, followed by M012 since Q is measurable, shows that every constant times 1_Q is integrable.

On the open set (ℝ^n\C)×int J the map is the constant q: compact C is closed in Euclidean space, and H006 gives equality there. At every point of this open set all positive-order derivatives of u are zero, since locally the difference quotients of a constant are zero, and this applies repeatedly to its derivatives. N001 supplies smoothness of every derivative. Thus for every r∈int J, e,e_t,u_t·u_tt,u_t·Δ_xu and the listed derivative products vanish outside C. For g_j(x)=u_t(x,r)·∂_{x_j}u(x,r), smoothness follows by finite products and sums of the smooth components. Both g_j and its derivative are smooth and zero outside C as well. All scalar functions in the output are continuous. Their nonzero sets have closures contained in the closed compact C, hence their topological supports are compact.

M007 applies to each of the continuous compactly supported scalar functions of F003 on ℝ^n, with Lebesgue measure finite on compact sets, and gives integrability. M008 on Q applied to the absolute value of each such function gives a finite bound, which may be enlarged to be nonnegative. Since the function is zero off Q, its absolute value is bounded everywhere by this constant times 1_Q. F002 and monotonicity of the integral give the absolute-integral estimate stated in the output. In particular t0∈int J, so e(·,t0) is integrable. The construction works for arbitrary t0>0 and proves the entire quantified assertion of the output. H002 ensures that every appearance of e is within its defining smoothness guard.

R003.text: Fix t0>0 and choose the matching C,R from N002. Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], Q=[−R,R]^n and η=t0/4>0. Then [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J. The box Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is compact by M014, viewed as a closed coordinate order interval in ℝ^n×ℝ, and lies in Ω. N001 gives continuity of e_t there. M008 applied to |e_t| on this box gives a finite upper bound. Enlarging it to be nonnegative proves the existence of a real B≥0 bounding |e_t| throughout this box.

Choose B from F001, and define the family D_h as declared. For fixed x∈Q and 0<|h|<η, apply M004 to r↦e(x,r) on the closed interval between t0 and t0+h, with constant B. Both endpoints are interior times of J. The derivative exists by N001 and is bounded by F001; its within-interval derivative equals that ordinary derivative on the nondegenerate interval. Whether h is positive or negative, M004 gives |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|. Division by |h| gives |D_h(x)|≤B. For x∉Q, N002 gives zero density at both times, so |D_h(x)|≤B 1_Q(x) everywhere. N002 also states integrability of this majorant. Each D_h is continuous and measurable and is integrable by linearity from the two integrable density sections of N002.

The pointwise limit in F002 is precisely the definition of the time derivative of e at (x,t0), supplied by N001. Apply M003 with spatial measure dx, real codomain, index h∈ℝ and filter of nonzero h tending to 0, F(h)=D_h and limit function x↦e_t(x,t0). This filter is countably generated: the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k for positive integers k form a countable neighborhood basis. F002 gives eventual strong measurability (continuous real functions), the bound, integrability of B1_Q and pointwise convergence. Therefore ∫D_h dx→∫e_t(x,t0)dx as h→0, h≠0.

For all sufficiently small nonzero h, integrability from N002 and linearity show ∫D_h dx=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. Both energies are the actual finite integrals, not merely total-integral defaults. F003 is thus the derivative limit for E at t0 and proves E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Substituting the formula for e_t from N001, and using finite-sum and scalar linearity on the integrable terms from N002, gives E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2Σ_j∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. All these integrals are finite by N002. Since t0>0 was arbitrary, this proves the output.

R004.text: Fix t0>0 and spatial index j, and choose matching C,R from N002, putting Q=[−R,R]^n. H001 gives n≥1. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). N001 gives smoothness of its factors; M001 on each j-coordinate line gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. N002 states that all three scalar terms are continuous, integrable, and zero outside C. Since C⊂int Q, the function g is identically zero near the boundary of Q. In particular its values on both faces x_j=±R are zero.

At fixed remaining coordinates, integrate ∂_{x_j}g first over x_j∈[−R,R]. The one-dimensional section of g is smooth; its derivative is continuous on this finite interval and hence interval integrable. M005 gives the integral as g at the upper endpoint minus g at the lower endpoint, zero by F001. To pass to the n-dimensional integral, M010 splits standard Lebesgue coordinates into the j-th coordinate and the remaining n−1 coordinates; its inverse is coordinate insertion. Thus the product measure is exactly dx, not an unspecified proportional measure. Apply M006 to ∂_{x_j}g times the indicator of Q in these coordinates. It is integrable, because by F001 the indicator does not change the function. Both product measures (Lebesgue on [−R,R] or on the full coordinate factors with the box indicator) are sigma-finite and hence s-finite. Integrating the remaining coordinates gives ∫_Q∂_{x_j}g dx=0. When n=1 the remaining space has dimension zero and measure one; the same assertion is precisely the preceding one-dimensional FTC.

All terms in F001 vanish off Q, so F002 and linearity imply 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Symmetry of the real scalar product and rearrangement give the asserted integration-by-parts formula, including finiteness from F001. Universal introduction over t0 and j proves the entire output.

R005.text: For every t>0, N002 gives integrability of e(·,t). N003 proves differentiability of E there and its derivative formula. For each such t substitute N004 into that formula and use linearity for the finite integrable sum, obtaining E'(t)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx−2Σ_j∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu) dx. N001 makes the last integrand identically zero. Thus E'(t)=0 for every t>0. H002 supplies the smoothness guard on the definitions of e and E.

For arbitrary positive real endpoints s<t, F001 gives differentiability throughout [s,t] and zero derivative there. M004 with real function E and C=0 gives |E(t)−E(s)|≤0, and therefore equality. If the endpoints coincide equality is immediate, and if their order is reversed exchange them. This proves E(s)=E(t) for all s,t>0. In invoking the native total-function M004, extend E by zero at nonpositive times; [s,t] is inside its positive domain so this does not affect any derivative. The defining energy retains coefficient 1 on both squares and there is no assertion at time zero. Together with F001 this is exactly P.
